newsitem.title: USA: Simpson jury orders $25 million in punitive damages.
newsitem.headline: Simpson jury orders $25 million in punitive damages.

text.p: Ending O.J. Simpson's civil trial on a note of retribution, a jury Monday ordered him to pay a staggering $25 million in punitive damages for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend.

The panel, which had already found Simpson responsible for the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman and slapped him with $8.5 million in compensatory damages, chose to punish him in the only way they could -- by ruining him financially.

Wrapping up the sequel to one of the most sensational murder trials of modern times, jurors demanded that the former football star pay $12.5 million in punitive damages to Goldman's divorced parents and an equal sum to the estate of Nicole Brown Simpson.

"Finding O.J. Simpson liable for the murders ... was one of the easiest decisions I have ever had to make," said juror No. 11, a white woman in her 30s, at a post-verdict news conference televised nationwide.

Most of the jurors told reporters they were convinced Simpson lied on the witness stand and that attorneys for the victims' families proved their case beyond any doubt. "We came to the conclusion that Mr. Simpson should not profit from these murders," the jury foreman said.
The verdict -- plus the surprisingly large damage award levied on top of it -- marked a stunning counterpoint to Simpson's 1995 acquittal in the brutal killings.

A mostly black jury gave him back his freedom in his criminal trial, but 16 months later a predominantly white jury was determined to take away whatever remained of the fortune he amassed in his years as a star running back, advertising pitchman, film actor and sportscaster.

Unlike the verdict last Tuesday, this time the jury did not act with unanimity. The only person with black ancestry on the jury -- a Jamaican-born man who is half Asian -- was the lone vote against punitive damages, and he was joined by a dissenting white juror who felt the award was too high.

Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki, the no-nonsense jurist who muzzled attorneys and banned cameras from the courtroom, granted a 10-day stay that prevents the plaintiffs from going after Simpson's money until his attorneys can challenge the verdict.

Simpson, who had steadfastly maintained his innocence, chose to be absent for the final moments of the four-month trial. The victims' families -- who brought the wrongful-death civil case against him -- filled the spectators' gallery but showed little reaction when the jury's decision was read.

"The money has never been the issue. It's been to make sure that one man, the man who murdered my son and Nicole, is held responsible in a court of law. And it has happened," Fred Goldman, the grieving father who pursued the case against Simpson like a man obsessed, told reporters.
But attorney Leo Terrell, a strong Simpson supporter, exploded in anger, saying: "This is wrong ... This verdict is illegal. I guarantee there's going to be an appeal."
Dozens of camera crews and scores of curious onlookers descended on the lawn of the Santa Monica courthouse, and television stations broke into regular programming to broadcast the news live.

The jury began its final round of deliberations on Friday after plaintiffs' attorney Daniel Petrocelli urged them to send a message that "You cannot kill two people and get away with it." But defence attorney Robert Baker appealed for leniency, arguing that Simpson was heavily in debt and had already been punished enough.

Jurors denied race had anything to do with their verdict against the black celebrity. But a black woman, the only African-American remaining in the pool of alternate jurors, said the plaintiffs had not convinced her of Simpson's guilt.

From their earlier verdict, it was clear all of the regular jurors believed Simpson was the knife-wielding attacker who slashed his ex-wife and Goldman to death outside her Brentwood townhouse on the night of June 12, 1994.

Jurors emerged last Tuesday from six days of closed-door deliberations to slap Simpson with $8.5 million in compensatory damages, payable entirely to Goldman's family for the loss of his companionship and moral support.
The panel then took only five hours before deciding on Monday to pile on a total of $25 million in punitive damages, which are designed to set an example for society.

The award to Nicole Brown Simpson's estate goes to her legal heirs, Sydney, 11, and Justin, 8, the children she had with her celebrity husband. They are now living with Simpson, but the damages will go into a trust fund that he cannot touch. The children get the money when they reach adulthood.

Jurors may have been influenced in their decision by the testimony of plaintiffs' financial experts who estimated Simpson was worth $15.7 million and could earn between $2 million and $3 million a year by cashing in on his notoriety.
For their part, Simpson's attorneys had asked jurors to believe their client was virtually broke even though he lives in a mansion, drives a Bentley and employs his own bodyguard.

Independent estimates of Simpson's wealth range from $3 million to $5 million. Experts say the victims' families could hound him for the rest of his life, garnishing 25 percent of his income and forcing him into a more austere lifestyle.
But before the plaintiffs can lay claim to even $1, the judge must review the verdicts. If he deems the amount excessive, he can reduce it.
